about.title: About
about.headline: I take the half of the frontend that usually breaks
body: I am Viacheslav Androsov, a frontend engineer with four years of production experience. I started with Web3 interfaces on outsourcing, moved through B2B and FinTech products, and now work on the core of a corporate low-code platform: the editor engine, undo across operations, the frame budget.

What interests me is not the mockup but what sits behind it: how the state is arranged, what happens between frames, why a table starts stuttering at five hundred rows and what to do about it. I work in both React and Vue — not "familiar with both", but two production codebases I had to switch between mid-week.

Almost everything I have built is under NDA and cannot be linked. So this site is arranged differently: every claim that carries a number is rebuilt as a demo you can run right here and watch the counter.

principles.title: Measure first, then write
principles.body: Optimising without measuring is guessing. Twice while building these demos the measurement showed that the "slow" version was in fact fast, and the demo had to be rewritten rather than the wording adjusted.

principles.title: Boundaries over polish
principles.body: FSD, public APIs per slice, a linter that catches an import going upwards. Fifty modules and three teams in one repository survive on hard boundaries; they do not survive on agreements.

principles.title: Tests where mistakes are expensive
principles.body: Not for a coverage number. A buffer collapse that quietly changes data is caught only by a property over generated sessions; a panel printing the wrong schema, only by a test tying it to the validator.

footer.builtWith: Built with Next.js, GSAP and a strict grid.

demos.vueNote: This demo runs as a real Vue 3 island inside a React page. Vue sits in its own chunk and is not part of the initial payload: the browser picks it up after the page has rendered, and the island mounts once the demo reaches the screen.
demos.reactNote: This demo is React, like the original. Its own chunk too, out of the initial payload, mounted once it reaches the screen.
demos.portNote: This demo is React; the original was Vue 3, so what is on show is the model rather than the framework. Its own chunk too, out of the initial payload, mounted once it reaches the screen.

undoRedo.title: Undo buffer
undoRedo.lead: Drag the blocks, add one, delete one, rename one. Every gesture writes actions into a single buffer, and the buffer collapses before it is sent.
undoRedo.connecting: Now pick the second block — the link appears, or goes away.
undoRedo.hint: Drag a block, or tap one to select it. A whole drag is one action — ⌘Z undoes the gesture, not a frame of it.
undoRedo.coverage: Six action types here, forty-odd in the editor. The mechanism does not count them.

canvasFps.title: The frame budget
canvasFps.lead: One scene, one animation, two ways of getting a frame onto the screen. Flip the mode and watch the counter: the difference is not the machine, it is what the code finds to do between frames.
canvasFps.canvas: A field of blocks and links
canvasFps.hint: The modes are measured one at a time: there is a single main thread, and two scenes side by side would fight over it. The first thirty frames after a switch are thrown away as warm-up. Hit pause and compare the “loop” line.
canvasFps.naiveNote: Block positions live in reactive state, and the frame repaints the whole scene through left/top — properties that go through layout. Then a pass over the links reads each block's rectangle and immediately places a link from it: measure, write, measure, write. Every write dirties layout, and every next measurement makes the browser recompute it synchronously, in the middle of the frame.
canvasFps.budgetNote: Same work — every block and every link is repositioned, with no cleverness about updating only what changed. Two things differ: coordinates come from the array instead of being read back off the DOM, so nothing forces a layout mid-pass; and only transform is written, which reaches the compositor without going through layout. While paused, no frame is scheduled at all.

txTable.title: A table under live data
txTable.lead: Five hundred transactions, and a mock socket changing statuses every second. The highlight is not decoration: a row lights up at the exact moment React repainted it. Turn virtualisation or memoisation off and watch what lights up.
txTable.hint: The data is synthetic: merchant ids are generated, amounts are random. What is closed is the client's code, not the render strategy.
txTable.note: Virtualisation keeps a couple of dozen rows in the DOM instead of five hundred, so scrolling stops depending on the length of the list. Memoisation solves the other half: a status update repaints one row rather than the grid. It only works because the update leaves untouched rows as the very same objects — memo on top of a fresh copy of the array would not save a single render.

dynamicForm.title: A form that knows its own rules
dynamicForm.lead: Switch the payout method and it is not just the field set that changes — so does the schema the form validates against. It is printed in full on the right: not a picture of the schema, but its source, built from the same rules the validation runs on.
dynamicForm.hint: The schema follows more than the method: for a crypto payout the address is checked against the network you picked — change it and watch the pattern. Values the new schema has no place for are dropped: an IBAN must not travel along with a card payout.
dynamicForm.note: The rules are written once, as a list. Both the Zod object that validates and the text beside it are built from that list. There is nowhere for them to drift apart — and a test holds it: the panel must print every rule the schema validates by.

liveRollup.title: Numbers that survive a change of scale
liveRollup.lead: One stream of events, two roll-ups. One rebuilds every bucket from the raw events; the other folds the level below it, the way most dashboards do. Switch the granularity and watch which metrics stay identical and which quietly drift.
liveRollup.chart: Two roll-ups of one stream, drawn over the same window
liveRollup.hint: Turn on the gap and the raw roll-up leaves a hole where the folded one draws a zero. Nobody measured nothing — the same lie a food tracker tells when it prints 0 mg for a nutrient it never had.
liveRollup.note: Sum and count are decomposable: a minute is the sum of its twelve five-second buckets, and no arrangement of buckets changes the answer. An average is not — it needs the weights, and the fold has already thrown them away. A percentile is not decomposable at all: there is no operation on twelve p95 values that yields the p95 of the minute. The dashed line is not an approximation. It is a different question, answered confidently.

foodMatch.title: The row you pick is the answer
foodMatch.lead: Type a food. The same rows of the USDA corpus, ranked twice: once by the obvious rule — the shortest name, the most measurements — and once by the rule the product actually ships. They disagree by a factor of three, and the panel on the right names the tie-break that did it.
foodMatch.substring: read the name as a substring
foodMatch.nothing: No food by that name in this slice of the corpus.
foodMatch.hint: “Buckwheat” is 343 kcal and “Buckwheat groats” is 118. Both names are beyond reproach, and the corpus cannot tell you which one a person meant — only the food group can. So the caller states whether this is a food eaten cooked, and the ranking follows. An apple is raw and stays raw: turn the flag on for it and watch the answer get worse.
foodMatch.note: The ranking is a sort with eight tie-breaks, and no model takes part in it: choosing the row is choosing the nutrients, and that decision has to be reproducible and reviewable. The rules read a name as whole comma-segments rather than words — “Cheese, Parmesan, dry grated” is grated parmesan, and a word search calls it dry. This code runs here exactly as it runs in production. What is cut is the corpus: 154 rows across 18 foods, so the demo can list every candidate it ranks.

guardrails.title: The agent proposes, the build disposes
guardrails.lead: Seven diffs an agent might hand you. Five gates decide. Four of the five are this project's own rules — the same lint patterns, the same Zod schema, the same locale check, the same regex the backend greps itself with — running here on a toy file tree.
guardrails.stopped: The diff does not go in. It is not a review that stopped it — the build does not produce an artefact.
guardrails.passed: Every gate is silent, and the diff goes in. A wall that never opens is not a gate, it is a wall.
guardrails.advice: No gate has an opinion about this one, so it goes in. Only the instruction file asked otherwise — which is exactly what an instruction can do, and exactly why anything costlier than this does not live there.

guardrails.hint: The messages are the ones the real gates print, in the language the tooling prints them — an English lint message does not become Russian because you are reading the site in Russian.
guardrails.note: An instruction is advice: a model can forget it, and a long instruction file stops being read whole. A gate is not. So anything costlier than a typo lives in something that fails — a lint rule, a schema parsed at import, a test that greps the module it belongs to, a payload ceiling in the end-to-end suite. This demo runs the rules, not the toolchain: there is no eslint and no tsc in your browser, and the file tree is a fixture. What is real is the rules themselves, and a test that holds each of these diffs against exactly the gates it claims — a guard nobody has seen trigger is not a guard.

accessMatrix.title: The row decides, not the role
accessMatrix.lead: Four roles over one queue of tickets. Every action asks the same question — is this allowed — and the answer depends on the row it is asked about: whose flat it is, who it is assigned to, whether the work is done. Switch the verdict over to a role check written in the component and it agrees with the rules right up to the first ticket belonging to somebody else.

rules.operatorRead: An operator reads every ticket in the queue.
rules.operatorAssign: An operator assigns a ticket while it is still new.
rules.dispatcherRead: A dispatcher reads every ticket in the queue.
rules.dispatcherAssign: A dispatcher assigns any ticket, at any point.
rules.dispatcherClose: A dispatcher closes a ticket that is assigned to them.
rules.accountantRead: An accountant reads every ticket in the queue.
rules.accountantInvoice: An accountant invoices a ticket once the work is done.
rules.residentRead: A resident reads tickets from their own flat.
rules.residentClose: A resident confirms work done in their own flat.

accessMatrix.ask: Press an action on a row — that is the component asking whether it is allowed.
accessMatrix.noRule: No rule grants it, and that is the whole answer. Nothing here was forbidden; nothing was permitted either.
accessMatrix.diverges: answers the role check gets wrong
accessMatrix.hint: A dispatcher and a resident may both close a ticket — the role says so, and the role is right. Which ticket is a different question, and only the row can answer it.
accessMatrix.note: The rules are one file: nine calls to can, one branch per role, so a new role is a branch rather than a search through components. The panel does not map verdicts to explanations by hand — it asks CASL which rule matched, so an explanation cannot drift away from the rule that produced it. The role check beside it is deliberately given no ticket to look at: that is the defect being shown, not a simplification of it. Where the two disagree is pinned by a unit test, because a divergence nobody counted is not evidence.

walletState.title: You be the wallet
walletState.lead: The left panel is the wallet, and you are holding it: approve, refuse, answer that a request is already open, move the network under a connected app. The right panel is the application answering. No extension is asked for and no wallet is connected — what is on show is the state the application keeps, and what it says when a provider hands it a number.

advice.idle: Nothing has been asked of the wallet yet.
advice.connecting: The request is open in the wallet. There will be no second window — this one is waiting for you, possibly behind the browser.
advice.wrongChain: The wallet is on a network this application does not work in. The connection is intact; the network is not.
advice.switching: The wallet is being asked to switch networks. It can refuse, and refusing changes nothing that already works.
advice.ready: Connected, on the right network, and nothing is pending.
advice.signing: The signature request is open in the wallet.
advice.rejected: The wallet refused. Nothing was sent and nothing was spent — you can ask again.
advice.pending: A request of this kind is already open. Asking again opens nothing: the answer is in the window that is already there.
advice.signed: Signed. The signature is in the application and the connection stayed where it was.

walletState.quiet: The wallet is also allowed to say nothing at all: leave a request unanswered and the application stays in its waiting state rather than deciding on your behalf.
walletState.hint: Refuse a signature and watch what does not happen: the connection stays, the network stays, and the application returns to the state it was in before it asked.
walletState.note: The original was ethers.js, and the part worth showing is not the call — it is the state around it. Six statuses and one transition table: an event a status has no transition for does not exist, so it cannot corrupt anything. Buttons on both panels are enabled straight from that table rather than from a second list of what is currently possible, which is why the demo cannot drift out of step with the machine. The provider codes are real ones — 4001 for a refusal, -32002 for a request already open — and the same code deliberately reads differently depending on where it arrives: a refusal while connecting sends you back to the start, a refusal while signing costs you nothing.
